body.text: in brief
• Top EU negotiators have said the UK will likely need to adopt much tighter conditions if it wants to return.
• The pathway to rejoining could take at least a decade, one expert has warned.

It's looking increasingly possible that United Kingdom Prime Minister Andy Burnham could attempt to reverse the 2016 decision to leave the European Union, commonly known as Brexit, and pursue a pathway of 'Bre-entry'.

However, the Labour leader would face an uphill battle to return his nation to the economic and political bloc, with top EU diplomats cautioning that the country may have to agree to significantly closer ties to regain the benefits of membership.

Indeed, a resumption of what had been considered a special position within the EU — including the retention of its own currency — is unlikely, according to one expert, who said he didn't expect to see the UK back in the EU "this side of 2035".

"Something radical would need to happen for that to happen any time in the next 10 years," Ben Wellings, professor of politics and international relations at Monash University, told SBS News. "Which, of course, something might."
Support among voters in the UK for rejoining the EU ranges from 57 to 61 per cent, with consistent majorities among those who say Brexit was a mistake and an overall failure.

However, champions of the move to leave, including former Conservative prime minister Boris Johnson and former senior cabinet minister Michael Gove, have said they would oppose any attempt to reverse the decision, threatening to make the campaign as divisive as it was a decade ago.
Will the United Kingdom rejoin the European Union?
Since taking over as party leader from Keir Starmer in July, Burnham has made it clear he is far more sceptical and outspoken about the impact of Brexit than his predecessor.

"Brexit has done more harm than good," Burnham told a Labour Party conference in September, using his speech to pledge four long-term strategic options the UK could pursue in its relationship with the EU.

The comment was a major break from UK leadership tradition, which has either been to talk up Brexit or largely ignore it. The PM has since made a series of critical comments about Brexit, describing it on Monday as "like the emperor's new clothes".

During a podcast appearance last month, he went further, asserting that the 2016 referendum was subject to interference from Russia, which he claimed UK intelligence confirms is still "instigating" political divisions in EU member states.

Later this week, Burnham will take part in a UK-EU summit aimed at "resetting" relations and forging closer ties. Both sides are hoping to secure three agreements: cutting red tape for food exports, linking the two sides' emissions-trading schemes and finalising a "youth experience" scheme allowing young people to move between the UK and EU for limited periods.
"I'm in a negotiation about improving the Brexit deal — that's what I'm doing this week. We'll see how it goes," Burnham told Sky News in the UK.
"And then we will consider whether there are options to further the relationship with the EU."
The four options Burnham has sought formal negotiations with the EU about are:
• Maintaining the UK's status quo position under its existing Trade and Cooperation Agreement
• Negotiating a comprehensive UK-EU Customs Union to remove tariffs and checks
• Re-entering the European Single Market
• Full re-entry to the European Union
Sticking with the status quo and refusing to seek closer renegotiation with the EU would be a "major dereliction of duty," Burnham has said.

However, these are thought to be long-term strategic goals, which Burnham has said would require an explicit electoral mandate. He has promised to take his plan to the people at the next UK election, expected before August 2029.

Wellings told SBS News that, even domestically, the idea is politically fraught, as the loyalties created through the Brexit vote and the populist ideas underpinning some of them "haven't gone away", as seen in the support for Brexit-instigator Nigel Farage's Reform UK party.
"I think people would hesitate to reanimate the bitterness of those divisions and its effect on public life," he said.
Would the European Union let the UK back in?
Currently, the UK is renegotiating its position with the EU at its third annual so-called "reset summit".

This month, the two sides are expected to sign off on a package of deals that will eliminate red tape on physical border checks of agricultural and food goods, which the UK believes could unlock some £5.1 billion ($9.98 billion) in trade growth.
The deal would also liberalise the movement of EU and UK citizens under 30 to live, travel, and study across the continent, while linking the EU and UK carbon markets.

However, top negotiators have said the UK cannot simply cherry-pick the EU benefits it wants and, over the next 12 months, the bloc is looking to freeze its position on the UK until the country can come back with a firm, stable offer.
"Clarity is what we need more than anything from the UK," one senior EU diplomat told The Guardian this week.
The EU's former chief Brexit negotiator, Michel Barnier, has consistently maintained that the door remains open to the UK, but that returning on pre-2016 terms is no longer possible.
"The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market," he said, referring to freedom of movement, capital, goods, and businesses.
The terms of re-entry to the EU would be significant to UK voters, Matthew Smith, head of data journalism at the YouGov UK polling organisation, has said.
The two top issues are whether the UK would be allowed to keep the pound and whether it would get back the 66 per cent reduction in financial contribution to the EU negotiated by Margaret Thatcher.
Both of these are thought to be out of the question and, if so, would significantly change voters' favourability of the decision.
However, Smith said rejoining the EU is not a top issue for many Britons, with immigration and the economy far outweighing it.

Still, the geopolitical landscape has shifted significantly since 2016, and Wellings notes it may just make overwhelming sense for the UK to align itself with Europe against an increasingly aggressive Russia and a currently anti-EU United States.
"There's a strategic logic that says yes ... as long as a radical right party doesn't come to power in, say, France or Germany," he said, eyeing a key French election early next year.
The "most likely outcome", Wellings said, is that a mandate to "negotiate some form of re-entry" will be included in the Labour Party manifesto taken to voters at the next general election.

The UK, unlike Australia, would not need a referendum to make such a decision and Burnham could gain a polling boost by campaigning for the option at the next election. From there, however, the path becomes less clear.
Finland became the fastest country to join the EU after submitting its application in 1992 and entering the bloc in 1995, fast-tracking a process that normally takes eight to 10 years.
Whether UK voters see the country rejoin within their lifetimes, Wellings said, very much depends on the length of those lifetimes.
